name: Littlewood's Law
statement: You can expect a one-in-a-million 'miracle' about once a month.
meaning: Given how many small events fill an ordinary life, an event that is individually a one-in-a-million long shot is, in aggregate, routine: roughly one a month. What feels like a supernatural coincidence is the statistically expected rate of rare events.
mechanism: The arithmetic: a person is awake and alert about eight hours a day and perceives, very roughly, one distinct 'event' a second (some thirty thousand a day). At that rate a million events accumulate in about thirty-five days, a little over a month, so a one-in-a-million event should turn up about monthly. It is a personal, per-month packaging of the law of truly large numbers: with enough trials, even wildly improbable outcomes become likely.

examples.text: A psychic who makes very many predictions will score some astonishing hits by chance alone; the misses are forgotten. The occasional uncanny hit is the expected rare event, not evidence of foresight.
People dream nightly; across billions of dreams, some will coincidentally match a later real event. A dream that 'came true' is a one-in-a-million coincidence arriving at roughly its expected rate.
As Penn Jillette put it, among eight million New Yorkers 'million-to-one odds happen eight times a day'. Events that are rare per person are common across a population.

variants.name: The law of truly large numbers
variants.text: The parent principle, formalised by Diaconis and Mosteller (1989): with a large enough number of opportunities, any outrageous thing is likely to happen somewhere. Littlewood's law is its per-person, per-month form.

variants.name: Not the law of large numbers
variants.text: A common confusion: the law of large numbers is a formal theorem about sample averages converging to the expected value (a different thing that merely shares part of the name).

whyItMatters: It is a standing antidote to the supernatural reading of coincidence: before treating a striking event as a sign, remember that striking events are statistically due. It reframes the miraculous as the ordinary output of large numbers plus selective memory.

working.text: across a life or a population, one-in-a-million events are not surprising; they are scheduled: treat a single uncanny event as expected, not as a message.
we notice and retell the hits and forget the vastly more numerous non-events; correcting for that selection dissolves most 'miracles'.

working.lead: Don't infer a cause from a coincidence
working.text: a striking match is what large numbers produce; it is not, on its own, evidence of foresight, fate, or the paranormal.

limits: The inputs (one event a second, eight alert hours a day, hence a million events in about thirty-five days) are illustrative assumptions, not measurements, and 'event' is undefined; the 'month' is really closer to thirty-five days, and a 'miracle' is arbitrarily fixed at one in a million for tidy arithmetic. Its attribution is also shaky: the popular monthly-miracle formulation, with this arithmetic, was set out by Freeman Dyson in 2004; Littlewood himself only used one in a million as a threshold for an impressive coincidence (a small Stigler's-law case).
misreadings: It does not claim miracles are impossible, or that anything mystical is going on: the opposite. It says rare events are statistically expected across enough opportunities, so a single astonishing coincidence needs no special explanation.
origin: Named for the Cambridge mathematician John Edensor Littlewood, who in A Mathematician's Miscellany (1953) used one in a million as the threshold for an impressive coincidence. The fuller 'law of miracles', with the waking-hours arithmetic and the one-a-month conclusion, was actually formulated by the physicist Freeman Dyson in 2004, drawing on Diaconis and Mosteller's work and attributing it to Littlewood.

sources.text: Littlewood, J.E. (1953). A Mathematician's Miscellany. — the one-in-a-million coincidence threshold.
Littlewood's law, Wikipedia. — the statement and the arithmetic.
gwern.net, "The Origin of Littlewood's Law." — the evidence that Dyson (2004), not Littlewood, formulated the monthly-miracle law.
